utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. I think we are full -- no, we are not full house. I don't -- yes, we are full house. Mr. Sarapa is behind the column. Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. The witness is here as well. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today we are going, hopefully, to finish with your testimony. Mr. Haynes, you still had a few minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, good morning to you. I've just got a few more questions to finish off with, and I'm going to start by asking if you could be shown P707 in e-court; English, page 9; and B/C/S, page 8. Mr. Vuga, you've seen regulation 7 before, and you might recall Judge Kwon asking you a few questions about who might be somebody of equal or higher ranking military rank to the army commander, but let's just look at that section together: Military police may not be used to perform duties outside of their needs and tasks unless authorised by the army commander or an equal or higher-ranking military officer. The question I want to ask you is rather different, which is, in your view would that authority have to have any formality? In other words, would it have to be in writing, or would it be sufficient that, for example, an acting commander were informed by his security officer that these instructions came from the very top?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, the acting person who was given authorisation to be able to decide about this matter, that is to say that the military police can be used and deployed outside its regular functions, does not get that authorisation from the security organs but the senior officer down the chain of command starting with the army commander, and this authorisation depending on the circumstances in which it is issued can be orally given if the situation is of an urgent nature, but this kind of authorisation is in principle granted in written form so that it can set up precisely the terms and what it refers to and the duration of the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuga. That's very helpful. Can we now, then, have a look at 1D1078 in e-court, please. And I'd like you to look at the first page so that you can recall the document, and then we will have a look at the end of it. Is that clear enough for you, Mr. Vuga? Can you see that document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. It is legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Zivanovic showed you this document sometime last week. It's a report from the command of the 5th Military Police Battalion of the Drina Corps. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you seen many other such reports at Drina Corps level from the command of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "many" is a flexible term, so I can't really answer that. What do you mean by "many"? How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a fair comment. Can we go to the second page? I just wanted to know whether from your observation it was standard practice in the Drina Corps for reports of the Military Police Battalion to be addressed only to the chief of security and the Chief of Staff, not the commander.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the way in which the military police was under control and command, it was through the security officer that they had to go to the commander. I have no other information. The Chief of Staff was informed of the activities because they -- this involves combat action and of course that to the operative part of the staff, they had to take note of it. Now, as to the Chief of Staff, this is not in contravention to cooperation between the security organs and the Chief of Staff when it comes to this type of report. However, the commander must necessarily have had a report of this kind as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on quickly, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If the commander is not listed as one of the addressees or one of the recipients, how would he come into possession of such a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had to have received it from the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Or directly from the commander of the unit of the military police. So there are two possibilities for that: One, that the commander of the military police directly reported to him; or that the report was -- reached him through the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you just guessing as those possibilities, Mr. Vuga?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the prescribed ways and duties in which this had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, prescribed where?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was regulated and prescribed in the instructions for applying the rules of service within the military police, where deployment is set out, as well, and this also implied this kind of information system and reporting system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave that there. I'm coming to my last small topic, and I'd like to have a look, please, at 3D396; B/C/S, page 40; and English, page 48. This is a diagram or schematic that you drew as part of your report in this case. I dare say you recall it, Mr. Vuga.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And before we go any further, the Zvornik Brigade was an infantry brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes, an infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the manner of drawing this diagram is quite standard. The solid lines are intended to denote lines of command, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. They are the lines of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the broken lines are intended to denote lines of functional or specialist control?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. Those lines are called, according to the regulations, the lines of control in the professional sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, it's your opinion, isn't it, that the military police in an infantry brigade are commanded indirectly by the commander of the brigade through the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This schematic or diagram shows otherwise. The commander commands the military police directly. It is subordinated to him, as is the security organ. The commander can choose via the security organ to accomplish certain assignments in which there would be space and need for professional management and guidance of the military police and professional supervision over the execution of the tasks assigned to the military police, and once again, based on choice he can directly issue assignments to the commander of a unit of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, this isn't the first time you've given evidence before this Tribunal, is it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not the first time, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the schematic I've put up on the screen is not the first report you've ever written for the purposes of giving evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not the first report, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have in e-court, please, 7D952; page 29 in both English and B/C/S. You can see the first page there. This is the previous report you wrote for the Vukovar case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. That is that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: For those of us who are reading it in English, we will have to read page 29 and then go over to page 30. So if the English page could be moved forward a little bit now. And I chose the words from this report to put to you that it was your opinion that in an infantry brigade, the military police is subordinated to the brigade commander indirectly, i.e. via the chief of the security organ. Do you not still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, what you've just shown us is not an infantry brigade. It is a guards motorised brigade, motorised guards brigade, which is different on all counts from a classical infantry brigade. So the schematics cannot be compared because the functions were quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look, then, please, at the same document 7D952; page 73 in the B/C/S; 90 in the English. I think the page is wrong in B/C/S, but it doesn't matter. We'll just look at it in English, please, if we can turn it the right way around. It says in the bottom right-hand corner of this diagram, which you drew for a report you wrote two years ago, that this is a schematic of the composition of the infantry brigade. So it's not a guards brigade. This is the composition of an infantry brigade. And can you see that in this diagram there is no direct line of command from the commander to the military police unit, and there is a solid line denoting command from the security organ to the military police unit. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we should see here, Mr. Haynes, is what infantry brigade it is here because the solutions were different and decisions were different because the composition of the cadres of the staff within the command of the brigade and communications was defined by the size of the tasks in hand. So all this corresponds to a specific brigade because the rules governing brigades envisages several types of brigades and caters to several types.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you've already agreed with me, Mr. Vuga, that the Zvornik Brigade was an infantry brigade, and this is your schematic for the structure of an infantry brigade. So that's answered that question, hasn't it? I just want to know why you drew this diagram in 2006 and a rather different diagram when you came to write your report for this case.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, fairly different. That isn't quite right. It's different only with regard to the possibilities of command and control over the military police, and this is in accordance with the regulations. According to the regulations, you can command and control the military police directly or through the security organs. So this "or" isn't excluded in this version, either, this alternative. It only depicts a given situation at a given point in time. There is an "or" here too, an alternative. Without changing the definition, you can include this possibility because this is a possibility for a commander, and it is also a commander's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, thank you for your time. I've got no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey? Colonel, you're now going to be cross-examined by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I need the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Tapuskovic, is that the same dossier the witness had when he was being examined in direct by you or by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are the same documents that the witness had in the course of his examination or in the course of the examination-in-chief, but if necessary the Prosecution can check the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I just asked the question. I knew what the answer would have been, but I just wanted to put it straight for the record. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone. I had asked the Defence if they could make the colonel's report available to him so -- if I asked him to look at it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, good morning.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, yes, as you've heard quite a few times over the last week, my name is Peter McCloskey. I represent the Prosecution. I would like to just, before I get into sort of my more planned cross-examination, ask you about a couple of things that just came out with Mr. Haynes. You had said in response when Mr. Haynes had 1D1078 up on the board that document that was not addressed to the commander, but you had said that that had had to be received by the commander from the security organ or the commander of the MPs. Can you explain that concept, why the commander had to have received such information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's easy to explain this idea because the chief of the security organ and the MP commander are directly subordinated to the commander, and the Chief of Staff is also subordinated to him, who also receives such a report, so there are three possibilities or, rather, there are three individuals who must have received such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But what is it about the job of commander that means the commander has to get this information? Why does the commander have to get this information? Why are you so sure when you get up there and say he had to receive this? What is it about the nature of command that makes this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there is the principle of unity of command. A commander had to receive reports for all those directly subordinated to him, reports on the work that they had to carry out in accordance with the law and in accordance with their rights to command. So this is the idea of singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. What is it about a military commander? I don't get all the information from all my subordinates. What is it about a military commander in his particular responsibility that makes you so sure he has to get this kind of information? Or why does he need to have this information, if that's a --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, a commander takes extremely important decisions, and he quite simply has to have access to all the available information without which it's impossible to assess the situation and without which one cannot take valid decisions. In such a situation, it wouldn't be possible to assume responsibility for such decisions. The singleness of command and the idea of subordination were the basic principles upon which the military organisation that I spent 36 years in was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You also -- just a minute ago, Mr. Haynes was asking you questions about the security officer using the military police and asking you about the commander's role, and in that you said something about that the authority starts with the army commander. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember that, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the army commander would take decisions about when and in which cases the military police could be engaged, to carry out tasks that weren't part of its regular tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's say the army commander we are talking about is General Mladic, and he passes an order down regarding the use of military police in some operation. What role of responsibility of any do the subordinate commanders have, and I want you to consider this to be a brigade -- an order that has to do -- starts with Mladic but ends up in the brigade, so the military police are doing something for the brigade. Where does the corps and the brigade commander fit into any responsibility for an order that is generated by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we have to distinguish orders from authorisations. An order is something that has to be carried out. When a commander issues an order, the subordinate has the duty to carry out such an order. Authorisation involves giving subordinate commanders the right to act in certain situations in which it is necessary for the military police to act and to carry out duties other than duties that it usually carries out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's talk about an order, then. Mladic gives an order that goes down to the military police. What role, if any, would the commanders in the corps and the brigade have in relation to that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a case, if an order was issued, such as you have described, it's the duty of subordinates to carry out the orders of their superiors, if we are talking about orders, not about authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would that apply to the Drina Corps commander and the brigade commander whose orders this went through to get to the military police of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would fully apply to the corps commander and commanders in units subordinated to him if they also included military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if I can interrupt here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's suppose if General Mladic had something to order or a specific assignment to be performed by the military police of Zvornik Brigade, would that order be passed through commanders or the chief of security or intelligence at the Main Staff, through security lines or command lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood your question, Your Honour. An order, such an order issued by General Mladic to his subordinate commanders, according to which they should use the military police or any other kinds of orders, such an order would pass through the line of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that same subject, let's say for some reason the commander is not found. Would General Mladic or General Krstic normally be able to trust their security officer to pass on their order to, say, the brigade commander? If they couldn't speak -- if the commanders couldn't speak or order each other directly, would a security officer be trusted enough to pass on General Mladic's order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in my experience, as far as I know and given what the documents state, a commander is always present. There is always someone who plays the role of commander, and he has the authority to perform the duties of commander at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you, and I understand that. I just ask you to look into a situation where the security officers are talking to each other. Would there be anything inappropriate about a corps or Main Staff security officer passing on to a brigade security officers the order of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Passing down orders through such a line could only concern professional issues in regard of the military police. Commanding excludes the possibility of interfering with this line of command at any level of the military organisation. This is particularly the case given the idea of singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to where I had intended to start, and I want to go into a little bit of the background, a little bit of your background a little more. Before the war in Bosnia, did you have any family connections to Bosnia? We see in the census a number of Vugas around the Gorazde area.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, my mother was born in the village of Vrbaska near Banja Luka in 1912; and when she was four years old, her family moved across the Sava to Slavonia. My only connection, well, is that fact and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And during the war in Bosnia, did you have any connections with the army, either at the time -- we know you retired in September but either before you retired or after you retired, did you go help out the VRS, the RSK folks any time during the war with your expertise or knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in the security department I was the assistant of the chief of the security department for the security organs in National Defence secretariats throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The connections I had in that field with Bosnia-Herzegovina were identical to the connections I had to other parts of the former Yugoslavia. They didn't have a specific character or nature of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about after you retired?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having retired and after the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and after the signing of the Dayton Agreement in the year 2000, I became involved in developing the idea of security for the Army of Republika Srpska. I was asked to carry out this work, and to the best of my abilities I did this. So all I did was within those limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So from September 1992 to when the war ended near the end of 1995, you weren't involved with the VRS in any way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. I had fulfilled my role before retiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, right before you retired, you were the assistant chief of security. Who was your boss? Who was the chief of security? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made a request to retire, on the 16th of March, 1992, the chief of the security administration of the national Secretariat for Defence was General Aleksandar Vasiljevic. And when I retired on the 30th of September, 1992, the chief was Major General Nedeljko Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was General Boskovic's boss when you retired?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Boskovic's boss was the then-Federal Secretary for National Defence. I can't remember who his superior was exactly at the time, but it was the Federal Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the Federal Secretary for National Defence's boss?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Federal Secretary for National Defence was a member of the parliament, and the Prime Minister was his boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think we need to go into that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Was a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Error in transcript. It is page 15, line 8. It was said "parliament." He said "government."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was corrected by the interpreter himself already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, before you retired in September of 1992, your position as the assistant chief would have given you a very good look at what had been going on from 1991 in Croatia, Vukovar, and what was beginning to happen in Bosnia in March of 1992; is that right? I don't want to get into all that, but I just want to ask you whether or not you would have had a pretty good look at all that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the events that took place -- well, I was responsible for controlling the organs of security in the secretariats of National Defence, as I have said. So it's difficult to obtain information, broad kind of information, in such a position. As an officer, what I can say is that I was informed, but as a member of the organs of security and as a chief -- as assistant chief, I didn't have sufficient information on other issues in order to be able to provide you with a satisfactory answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You wouldn't have known the name of the Seselj's paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In the Vukovar case when I started with the report or work on the report, I obtained information that I had no previous knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've just told us you requested to be retired in March of 1992. I think you were only 54 years old then. Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did what you had seen happen to the former Yugoslavia play a role in your deciding to request retirement at such a young age?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was born in Croatia. Don't hold it against me if I tell you a detail from my biography that has always been of key importance. In 1943 and 1944, I was imprisoned in an Ustasha camp, and all my subsequent cares and concerns in Croatia bore the trace of this experience until the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was established. In that country, I became a citizen equal to all other citizens. This was my main concern in life, and this was my life-time desire. It was my life-time desire to see such a country in existence, to see the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. When this country was broken up and the war in Croatia came to an end, it was my conviction that my mission within the army had come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you work with or get to know General Mladic during your time in the JNA and VJ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only met him accidentally on one occasion. I greeted General Mladic on one occasion. He returned the greetings, and that is all. I had no other kind of contact with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about General Tolimir? He, as you've already told us, was the Main Staff head of security and intelligence from very early on. You gentlemen were coming from a similar background. What knowledge or contact did you have with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as for General Tolimir, the situation is somewhat different. General Tolimir is ten years my junior, and when I was an officer in the security organs and when I held the positions that I held, General Tolimir did not yet hold positions that would have involved me having close or direct contact with him in the course of performing my duties. But as a security officer and given all the duties I had to perform within the army, I knew more or less all the officers in the JNA who had security-related tasks to perform. And as a result, I also had contact with General Tolimir or knew General Tolimir on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollections of my meeting with Colonel Beara is linked to the period of 28 years ago. I and Colonel Beara met for the first time in Split when he was on duty there in the navy. I don't know his position exactly, but it was a very brief encounter because I had come within the composition of a team which was engaged in professional supervision of the work of the security organs in the navy command of the SFRY, the then-SFRY, of course, within the composition of the JNA as a whole. And since then, well, that's when I first met Colonel Beara, and I've known of him since then. I have known about how he developed professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to get into the time period of 28, 30 years ago. I think that was the height of the Cold War, 1960s, early 1970s. Were you working in counter-intelligence with Colonel Beara? And I won't ask you about that work. I know you're probably not even allowed to tell me about it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have anything to tell you because I never worked with him in counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of security work, then, if it's not counter-intelligence did you work with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I never worked on other security affairs within the frameworks of the service except in counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your report that - you were talking about interrogations - that coercion could be used, but it had to be approved by someone high up the line in the ministry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term in my testimony, the application of force, the approval of force and application of force, to the best of my recollections, I didn't say that. Now, I'd have to check that, look it up, but if it was wrongly interpreted, that's another matter again. So "coercion" is not a word I use, and that was absolutely not resorted to in my work or in my testimony. That was not a method to be used. Not only was it prohibited, it was absolutely not allowed to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence work, interviewing opposing spies in the Cold War, coercion was never used? Is that what you're saying? I won't get into this, but I just want to make it clear that you're saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is very ambiguous question about Cold War and coercion was never used in Cold War. I don't know that the expert knows everything about Cold War and coercion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would strike him off as an expert if he didn't know about those subjects, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I was just responding to your comment. Let me try to help you so you can see what I was referring to because, yeah, we do have translation issues here. It's your report. It's -- I believe it's the Popovic report. It's in section 2.13. It's -- do you have that in front of you? I'm sorry, because we better get it out because all I have is the English -- the English version. It's page 5 of the English, but it is under section 2.13 in the B/C/S, and it's just the first two or three pages of the B/C/S, if -- if that can be pulled up on the screen. Do you see that section, 2.13, in your report? And I'll get a 65 ter number, if -- 3D396, thank you. And I'm reading the part that starts out with "regard to regulating relations in the security domain".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Vuga has hard copy in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He can't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't managed to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I've got a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is in first binder of Mr. Vuga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the first binder, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But the thing is -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 5, B/C/S. It's that paragraph, and it's 2.13. It's page 5 in the English. It's the same for the Nikolic report and the Popovic report. It's under the section, "Security provisions and the law on the defence of the RS." 2.13: "With regard to regulating relations in the security domain, the Law on the Army of the RS does not contain any provisions or paragraphs regulating the field of security concretely in detail. In this domain, only the section covering the use of weapons by authorised personnel in the military security service and military police is concretely prescribed." Article 26 of that law states, "Authorised military personnel and the military security service and the military police may use, while performing military security or military police duties, weapons and other means of coercion under conditions prescribed by authorised officials of the Interior." The word -- I can't help you with the actual word, but I think you got the gist of that. "Coercion under conditions" -- I don't think anyone is saying coercion is necessarily a problem with dealing with these issues, sir, so my question is, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what is missing here, when you were talking about coercion, under conditions prescribed by law. That's the missing phrase, which means that there are specific authorisations which are prescribed, regulated, for individuals conducting security business, what those conditions are, and under what conditions the security organs are able to apply 5 authorisations and 14 authorisations that they have right to apply, and that is prescribed by law. So there is no application of force or coercion outside that, and that does not include interrogation of spies and uncovering them. These are different conditions and are beyond the context of this discussion and has nothing in common with either the Cold War or the methods of work of the security organs, but it has to do with authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I just pulled this out of your report, so my question is and is exactly that: What legal forms of coercion were prescribed that you may have had to get authorisation from the minister?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, coercion is prescribed by the law governing internal affairs, which was voted on and passed in parliament, and it wasn't the ministry that provided such authorisation. The law or that law underwent parliamentary procedure, and it provided for the fact that, as regards those who do not -- those people who do not, at the request of the security organs in performing their professional duties, that is to say establishing identity or if they are -- they are protecting someone, they have five authorisations at their disposal for them to be able to conduct that, and among those is the use of weapons in strictly prescribed situations, and among others if they are not able to repel an illegal act against themselves or an individual under their protection and whose duty it is, that is the security organ's duty is, to protect that individual, then they can resort to et cetera. So this is a point in time when the security organ is authorised to use weapons as the last resort at their disposal, and they also have the right before that to use physical force to overcome an attacker; that comes first, to caution him and warn him beforehand, and to identify the person or establish his identity. So these are the authorisations in the performance of their duty. Outside those authorisations, there are no other conditions and situations in which the security organs may avail themselves of the use of force, and I stated this because it was one of the conditions for criteria to be prescribed for admittance into the security organs and service because this is a very important point, an important situation, and they must be -- it must be assessed very well and evaluated. The situation must be properly evaluated, and that is something not everyone can do. That also refers to the policemen on the beat in the street when he has the right to use his weapon in situations that prescribe this. So it's a general provision, a general regulation, providing for authorisation to organs of the Interior, not only the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we all fully understand a police officer or a military police officers and his rights to use force and deadly force in is various situations. What got me is the word "coercion." Can you give me an example of coercion that a security officer would have to seek authority for, coercion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no special authorisation. He's on duty, engaged in an assignment which provides for the use of force. So if he is providing security, for example, for an individual, for a person, or security for special importance buildings or premises, so in carrying out his duty he comes across a problem in which he is forced to resort to these sorts of authorisations, which are given in the order stipulated, and according to the different levels and degrees, he in the performance of his duties is authorised - he doesn't need permission - he is authorised to do that. Now, outside those situations, in talking to people, interviews, collecting information and in all other situations, which he does in the course of his duty, there is no application of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would a security officer in an interrogation have to seek approval in order to use the technique of keeping a light on 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He cannot receive such authorisation unless it is provided for by law or something that is applied, such as the Law on Internal Affairs. So he cannot seek or be given such approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you -- go back a little bit. Did you come to know General Gvero during your career?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. McCloskey. For a very brief period of time, I worked in an organisational unit headed by General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the organ for political affairs, for political work, and I was there for a very short period of time, even less than two months, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991 -- 1990 or 1991. It was for just a short period, so I have not got any specific recollections about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why were you there so short a period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for such a short period because it was a period when I came from another structure where I had been working temporarily and was going back to the security administration, which was being harmonised and dovetailed at the time with the newly arisen situation and requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the job of political affairs, 1991, did that have remnants of the eastern bloc Soviet political affairs, commissar, political officer in the unit situation? Do you understand what I'm asking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't have that kind of character. It was a period of time when two important reorganisations in the Yugoslav People's Army were taking place. The first was that the Yugoslav People's Army should de-- become depoliticised, That is to say, to throw politics out of the JNA, and for the JNA to become a non-political or be set on non-political foundations, and that the JNA should be defined in the new situation as non-ideological and extra-party organisation engaged in the defence of the country. So it was during that periods of time that I for a brief period was where I said I was a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about General -- now General Miletic? Did you get to know him or work with him at all?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for General Miletic, I never worked with him. I didn't know him except for a chance meeting. I don't know when it took place. I can't remember, but I do remember having met him briefly once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Vujadin Popovic. However, I was a lecturer in the education centre for security, and many people passed through that institution, over 2.000 over a given period of time. So from what I heard from Popovic by talking to him, he remembers me as a lecturer from those days. Nothing more than that. So I can't tell you anything more about or have nothing else to say about that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you were able to talk to Lieutenant Colonel Popovic in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity of talking to Lieutenant Colonel Popovic before I began preparing my report because I had to establish what my task was, what it was I had to do from the professional point of view, the point of view of my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did Colonel Popovic tell you what your task was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him what my task could be if he accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that that task would be acceptable in as far as I explained it to him, and that's how the task appears in my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to him about the details of your report, the rules, how they were applied in the RS at the time, some of these key days that you've talked about, these key issues that you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. I analysed the documents, the regulations, and conducted a comparative analysis to see what was in the documentations and regulations in order to identify points in common, common substance and solutions, and to make my own assessment and evaluation independently on the basis of the facts that I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why didn't you speak to Colonel Popovic on these issues?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was of the opinion that the circumstances in which Lieutenant Colonel Popovic found himself were not conducive to, from my point of view and suited to from my point of view, the formation of a comprehensive picture, the way I thought that this should be done as an expert myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, for example, you testified --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example -- for example, because a lot of time had gone by, one loses from sight some very important circumstances that took place at a time when the events took place, and it was no longer possible to view them realistically, from this passage of time and this vantage point, so my picture about everything that I did would or could be incomplete in a way or in certain sections even incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of the things you've talked about in your testimony, you said that relating to the separation of military-age men, you said it would be the duty of the security branch to work with the MPs to make sure that that job was done right and done correctly. And did you speak to Colonel Popovic about that, whether he in fact acted under what you said was his duty? That would have been a perfect time to ask him what really happened.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to these matters, I did not ask Colonel Popovic about them because that would have been a lesser portion or - let me put it this way - conditionally speaking, a very small part of the work he did. So I didn't attach that much importance to this, but I mentioned it as one of the things -- one of the jobs that he could perform under certain circumstances, of course, in the prescribed manner. As to the rest, I thought it would be established on the basis of other sources because the documents that I had did not contain such information, so other sources could be used, but as far as my profession is concerned, and my evaluation and assessment of work based on documents from the aspects of establishing the correctness of work would not have done that. So that is a question that is up to the Court to decide, up to the Trial Chamber to assess, and that was the reason and substance of that position that I took, my attitude and position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Drago Nikolic? Did you have a chance to talk with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My talk with Drago Nikolic was identical to the one conducted with Lieutenant Colonel Popovic with the proviso that before meeting Drago Nikolic and in talking to him -- well, I had no contact with him, nor did I have any fuller information about him, from the aspects of having an insight into his development and his work as a security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, your lack of contact with both these men, Drago Nikolic and Vujadin Popovic, are you saying that was specifically your decision based on you alone?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My decision was based on experience, experience from my previous work in compiling an expert report, and I thought that the best way of going about it given my position was to offer an expert professional view and assessment and conclusions about the regulations and duties that in conformity with those regulations were to be implemented, and I found them to be most reliable in the documents and material which was not subject to change, to alteration, which remained the same, remained the way it was at the time when it was being realised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you talk with Momir Nikolic and help him in preparing his case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did talk to Momir Nikolic as well. I talked to him about -- well, I didn't know him, so I needed him to tell me something about himself, what duty it was that he was performing, because it was the principal duty in the brigade which I as an expert studied for purposes of this case, these proceedings. The situation was the same when I talked to Momir Nikolic, but that work for well-known reasons and based on my testimony were not placed before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Meaning you knew he pled guilty?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to review his statement of facts that he made pursuant to that guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a chance to see that beforehand. I had it in my hands when everything was over and when the judgement came into force at the second instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right, but in preparing your reports for these gentlemen, you had Momir Nikolic's statement of facts pursuant to that plea?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an insight into that. However, Momir Nikolic, on the 3rd of April when we met told me that I should work in the way I have explained to you, so that on the 27th or after the 27th of April, he pleaded the way he pleaded. Now, between Momir Nikolic and myself, there is a view of all this, a vision of all this, which does not provide me with sufficiently reliable grounds for me to be able to conclude on a reliable basis things that I can use for writing a proper and correct report. So that was the reason why I did not take into consideration his statement of facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just -- last question because I see it's break time. You're also working for and set to testify in the state court for Milorad Trbic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I did not work on that. There was a discussion between me and his Defence counsel, which is still ongoing, this exchange, and I did not wish to include that exchange until I completed this particular testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Colonel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break of 25 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, one last -- on this issue before we get into more substantive material, have you been speaking at all to General Tolimir or his people about working for him in his upcoming case?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. Such things have never been discussed. The subject was never broached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you spoken to General Tolimir since his arrest?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. All I did was say that General Tolimir should be informed of my presence here, and it was only at the end of my testimony that he could meet me or I could meet him, if he was interested in such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any interest from him? Got any plans to see him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't received any feedback information for the moment. That's the situation at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the last information you received on this topic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have just said. I haven't received any other information. I'm waiting. Perhaps I'll receive information before I leave. If not, I'll leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did you pass the information on to to connect with General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through -- I passed this information on through Mr. Erol who welcomed me when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He works for the Tribunal in the victim and witnesses unit. I think that's the term. I don't know the exact term because I received it in translation, but he works here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go now -- I want to ask you about one of the rules. I don't want you to have to get into that too much depth because I think you've talked quite a bit about it and explained yourself. But relating to the rules of the security branch, I think you explained very well the professional relationship that a security officer would have with the military police unit and that it was part of the security officer's job to propose to the commander, the security officer's commander, on the best uses of the military police. So what I want to ask you about is when the security officer makes a proposal about some use of the military police, and the commander - let's say brigade commander - decides to act on that proposal and turns it into an order, what then is the security officer's duty in seeing to it that that order is carried out? And the other day on page 23060, line 5 and 6, you said something -- you said that the security officer can give professional guidance to the military police on how best to execute what the commander ordered. Is that -- is that right, in the context of the question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I did not see in your report where you explain how this works, so could you explain in a little more detail, given this situation, the -- what would the security officer do in providing guidance to the MPs to get the job done according to the proposal and now order of the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the question, but perhaps it wasn't really noted because I went into detail in the course of my testimony. When testifying in general, you can lose sight of certain important details, so I'll go over it to the extent that this is necessary. I won't repeat everything. First of all, the security officer is the most qualified individual to assess threatening activities, and on the basis of the information he obtains he can identify tasks that should be assigned to the military police given the duties that MPs have to perform. He has to command and control and guide the military police together with the company commander, and so he should be in a position to inform, one, of what the military police can succeed in doing when carrying out a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but there is I think a fairly significant error in the transcript that I ought to clear up with you. It says that the security officer has to command and control and guide the military police. Did you mean to say that the security officer commands the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, that's not the right word. Professional guidance is what is involved. It's not command -- a matter of commanding. Commanders command. It's the command of an MP unit. Well, you have the organ of security and the commander of a military police units. They have common information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We understand that. The term "rukovodjenje" is being translated sometimes as "command," but it's now supposed to be "control."

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rukovodjenje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm sorry to interrupt. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your intervention. The commander of an MP unit -- what the commander of an MP unit knows is essential as well as what the security organ knows, and on the basis of that information you have a suggestion that is formulated and forwarded to a commander, and on the basis of that suggestion the commander will then decide on what is important at that point in time and will then assign tasks. I can provide you with an example, if you like. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We understand that. What -- the examples I need you to provide me with is what role, if any, the security officer has in facilitating the commander's orders or making sure that it happens. What role does the security officer play, if any, given that it may have been his proposal in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. Well, his role follows a different course in this case. He has to monitor the way in which what has been suggested is being implemented, and given the commander's order, in light of the commander's order, he has to intervene as a professional, and he has to ensure that the tasks are carried out in an effective manner, and then he must inform the commander of the fact of the situation. He must inform him of the role he played as far as the role he played when he suggested that action be taken. So first you make the suggestion, and then you have to monitor how the task is being carried out. You have to intervene to ensure that the commander's order is being respected, that it's being implemented, and then you have to inform about what has been accomplished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I see that a part of the answer of the witness is not translated properly. It is at page 33, line 1 to 12. He said that security organ just have to intervene in professional aspect of the carrying out of order, commander's order, but not as professional. It was translated as "professional."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he didn't use the word as a professional?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. He used the words, in the professional aspect or [Interpretation] "In the professional aspect."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you confirm that, Colonel? Let me read it to you as we have it here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His -- yeah, but I want to make sure how it fits in now because it's still not clear to me. "He has to monitor the way in which what has been suggested is being implemented, and given the commander's orders, in light of the commander's order, he has to intervene as a professional, and he has to ensure that the tasks are carried out in an effective manner." What's wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, "professional," that's not very specific. We are talking about the act for which he is professionally responsibility. Professional is a bit different, but professional responsibility is a little more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted you to clear that up for us, to make sure that what Mr. Zivanovic raised was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have again a wrong translation because the word nadlezan, Serbian word nadlezan was translated, and "responsibility." It is the proper Serbian word odgovoran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's nadlezan? How should it be translated, nadlezan?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is in competence of security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think much is changed by any of that, Colonel, but I'd like to ask you. Let's say the security officer sees the military police doing something not the way it had been envisaged and he has to intervene. When he intervenes, can he issue instructions to the military police that were consistent with the commander's orders and his previous proposal?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was an important part of his role as an organ who had to guide and monitor the situation. He could issue requests in this respect. A request that one act and abide by the commander's order and to act in the way prescribed so he can make such a request. He cannot change a commander's order but within the limits of the order, he can exert his influence to ensure that this task is professionally carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: May be translation, but what is a better word for what he can do, "request" or "instruct"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a request, demand, it's like instructions. Can't be anything else, but it's a demand in the sense that you have to respect the commander's order. That's the professional part of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when a security officer comes to the commander of the MP and gives a -- and intervenes and makes an instruction to that commander, the MP, is that commander, the MP, required to follow that instruction?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions issued within the limits of a commander's order -- well, they have to be implemented in a professional way, and the commander of a military police unit is obliged to act on these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So whatever we call it, the MP commander is going to do it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's his duty to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Go to another topic for a little while. In your report, you spend a fair amount of time talking about the 28th Division and some of the bad things they were doing from 1992 to 1995, and sometimes you used the term "sabotage" and "terrorism" together. I want to ask you about one -- one comment you made in your report. It's at page 3, paragraph 1.17, and I can give you a -- it's 3D396 again. It's page 5 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S. It's probably easier -- since you haven't been able to find your report, I'll try to just give you the page. And take a look at paragraph 1.17. You state the following: "Experience has confirmed that the organisers and perpetrators of destructive activities [threats] do not have any moral, legal, or methodological restrictions and that they are comprehensively perfecting their destructive activity." Now, we know that you went on to talk quite a bit about the BiH army and the 28th Division specifically. Who if anyone are you referring to when you say the organisers and perpetrators of destructive activities have no moral, legal, methodological restrictions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this part of the report is the general part that focuses on problems that had been identified of a very long period of time, that I spent working within my field, the field that I worked in, and just so happens that I still work in this field. So this is a position based on investigating and following events, global events and local events as well. Each event, each specific event, does not have the characteristics of this general experience. It's individual. It has -- or they are individual and they have their own characteristics, but when you look at this within the context of one's general experience, it does fall under such a description. That's why you have this paragraph here. The entire view of the problem has been defined more specifically in terms of risks and threats. The risks and threats that are referred to here were subsequently analysed and become identifiable on an individual basis. So that is the sense of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Most of us would agree with you in that if you were describing terrorists, but are you suggesting that all the activities of the 28th Division in this time period were acts of terrorism or acts committed by terrorists?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Later, one moves on to documents, and these documents were analysed and relate to the 28th Division in particular. The 28th Division isn't referred to here, but terrorism is and problems that are related to terrorism and its appearance. The 28th Division is a different matter. It was analysed individually and on the basis of the documents that I had. There is nothing here that I did not find in documents and that is not part of the assessment on what was in accordance with the regulations on the application of war law and what amounted to violation of such law. So it's in this respect that one can analyse what the 28th Division is, but in this general part we can only deal with the part that has something in common with this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I -- I didn't see in your report any real problems or bad conduct carried out by the VRS in this time period. Would you say you're objective in this review? But very simply; we don't need a long answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules and regulations imposed limits on me, so I could not deal with the problem of the VRS, and so if I had been assigned a task to analyse something else, well, then I would have used other rules and regulations, and I would have analysed something else. But this wasn't the task assigned to me, and I can't assess the threats on the Muslim side. You should have to analyse the documents from the Muslim side for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go over a few documents and see if we can get your take on it, a few VRS documents. Let's start with 65 ter number 29. It's page 5 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S, and this is going to come up on the screen, Colonel. This is a document by General Mladic dated 19 November 1992, called, "Directive Operational number 4." And it lays out several tasks for the various corps at that time, and I hope they can help you -- I'm sorry that that's such a bad copy. But I want -- I'll read you the key part of the Drina Corps section, is what we are looking at. "From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad [the dam], Zvornik, and the corridor while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." Now, have you seen this document in the preparation of your testimony or report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. What I wanted to ask you is we see here that Mladic wants to force the enemy to leave, which I understand, but then it says, "Together with the Muslim population." Based on your knowledge, did the Muslim civilian population present some sort of security threat that would justify an order like this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the broad view of my expert report. It would open up a new security dimension, the appearance of Muslim civilians that accompanied the armed forces when attacking inhabited settlements in order to loot and destroy property of the civilian population in the territory where there was a conflict. And this created a security problem, not only for the armed forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, I can stop you there because I'm not talking about looters and villains that are with the army in their -- in their raids. What I'm talking about is villagers, people that lived in the villages of Eastern Bosnia, of Kamenica, Cerska, the areas around Birac, Zepa. I'm talking villagers, farmers, kids, old ladies, men, all the people that are going on their daily lives. That's what I'm asking you. Did they -- those people living there during the military operations to beat the Muslim army, is there some sort of security reason to justify their removal from the area, the civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as for the security reasons, I have addressed them. I spoke to you about them precisely, not military looting, if I can put it that way, or unnecessary destruction of targets without any military necessity. But of all the accompanying sometimes mass presence on -- of non-military forces from among the civilian population who made up what I said and to what I exclusively attached a security dimension within the frameworks and in the extent to which they deserved that. Now, as for this portion of the population that you're referring to here, on that occasion I did not speak about that as a security problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I understand it, but that's the problem with cross-examination. Sometimes lawyers ask you new questions. So can you -- in thinking about this, is there some sort of security issue in relating to these old ladies and kids and farmers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question has been answered twice. He spoke about the Muslim civilians on page 39, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. This is obstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It is pure obstruction, Ms. Fauveau. Let him answer the question, please. Colonel, could you answer the question? And please answer the question. Don't try to beat around the bush or go around it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not understand what you meant by beating about the bush or going around it. I would like to know how you think that I sidestepped this because I'm always ready to provide an answer to the best of my ability, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're specifically being asked about a particular part of the population, women, old women, and that, if they ever constituted a security problem. Please answer that question. That's part of the question, and then the rest, Mr. McCloskey can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to that part of the question, the answer given was that they weren't the object of security considerations and were not a security problem. So up above is the answer to the question. So I was a little taken aback when you said I hadn't answered it. They weren't a security aspect. They weren't a problem or the subject of my considerations. So they cannot be taken -- it cannot be taken as a security problem in my response and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. What military justification can you think of, then, if these aren't a security problem, to remove these people from the area of Birac, Zepa, Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have an insight into the military situation in Republika Srpska for me to be able to provide you with arguments, and I really have no military justification for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the expert, Mr. Vuga, did not deal with the problem of Gorazde and Zepa and Birac, but he is a military expert in the security field, and that is what he deals with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Do you wish to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I absolutely disagree. His report is rife with issues that happened in this area of Eastern Bosnia, and the activities of Naser Oric are all over Birac, the Birac area, which is a broad area of Eastern Bosnia precisely where we are talking about. However, he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the question is rather unfair towards the witness. Indeed, the text referred to by the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, continuing with her and that kind of comment, the witness and I, can we remove the witness if we are going to go into this kind after dialogue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, but if you insist on it. Colonel, can you please remove your headphones for a short while? And one moment -- can you put them back? I think we asked him before and he said no. Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please remove your headphones. I asked him because earlier on I think I heard him speak in English to the usher. I'm just saying it. I don't know whether he's understanding or not now, but earlier on I heard him from here speak in English to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My particular concern in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Something like that. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- conclusions that I'm being unfair to the witness, these kinds of things that, you know, may mount up or -- you know, we don't want to inflame the witness with such comments. I've got to spend some time with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what she has to say. So far to me she hasn't said anything that is irregular or highly irregular. Let's hear what she has to say. If she outsteps, then we'll stop her as we have before. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, President. The Prosecutor referred to a specific text that mentions the civilian population. In that text, there is no farmer, no person, no women or older people. It is the entire civilian population. Earlier on, the witness said why the civilian population may be a security concern. Now, if you pick a specific population out of that civilian population, the elderly women, the elderly people, he said that that segment did not cause a security concern, but he said that as such, the civilian population could be a security concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think I won't comment, of course, but -- and I don't think we need, at least I don't need to hear your comment on that. I don't know. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are going to move on. Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He answered the question, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Colonel, all right, we are going to move on. Let him take you back to the question. The question -- there was an objection from Ms. Nikolic. There was an objection from Ms. Nikolic to which he, Mr. McCloskey, had responded, and then Madam Fauveau intervened. Yes, you had put a question which had been answered, so you can put your next question, Mr. McCloskey. Your last question was, "Thank you, Colonel. What military justification can you think of, then, if these aren't a security problem to remove these people from the area of Birac, Zepa and Gorazde?" And he had answered, "I do not have an insight into the military situation in Republika Srpska for me to be able to provide you with arguments, and I really have no military justification for that."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question on this point, Colonel. Along with that population I described of the women and children and non-combatants living in these villages, there were many times mosques. Did the mosques in these villages where the army and the civilians were inhabiting, did those mosques after the combat was over, the mosques that remained standing after the combat was over and the Muslim military is gone and the civilians are gone, did those mosques represent any kind of a security threat to the VRS or the RS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my colleague has provided both -- has asked the question but provided the answer, as well, to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Colonel, could you answer the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither the mosques nor the churches nor any religious sites in general are military targets nor a security threat on either side or on any side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let's go on to another document. We are now getting into the period of May 1993 where you talked about in your report and testified about some of the things the 28th Division was doing outside the enclave, and I just want to show you a document, 65 ter number 3499. And it should come up. If you're having any trouble reading it, I can also hand you a nice clear copy. And this is, as I said, from 31 May 1993, to the TG Jazz 1 [phoen] command, attention Colonel Vukota Vukotic or Lieutenant Colonel Milan Urosevic, and it's from the deputy commander of the Drina Corps at the time, Colonel Milutin Skocajic, and it says, "Lieutenant Colonel Urosevic received a verbal order from the commander, Colonel Milenko Zivanovic, to demolish the water-tower and tank in the area of Zeleni Jadar [water supply system for Srebrenica]. Since this has not been done so far, this task is to be executed immediately, by June 1 1993 at the latest, and it is to be presented to the public as if the Muslim forces did it. During the execution of the task, strictly take care of safety of personnel and our forces in order to prevent any consequences. Upon the execution of the task, inform this command in writing." Was this a document you had a chance to review as you were looking in this time period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't have this document in my hands, nor did I analyse it.
