utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did this water tank, in your view, pose some sort of security threat to the Muslim -- excuse me, to the VRS forces, and I'm sure you know Zeleni Jadar at the time was within the enclave as the Muslims held.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I analysed, this wasn't a document that I had, so as such, alone, it could not have been the subject of my analysis. It isn't part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are going to have a lot that may not have been talked -- you may not have talked about -- well, not a lot. We are going to have some things that you haven't talked about, but that's what I say. You talked a lot about the activities of the Muslim units. Now I'm going to ask you to talk about the activities of some of the VRS units. That's fair game, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that my task, the assignment I had, was taken out of context and brought to a completely different set of assignments that I did not have within my own task. It was my task to analyse the function of the security organs within the Army of Republika Srpska, in the Drina Corps and the Zvornik Brigade, and it was -- and my task was defined to begin with. Its parameters were defined. So it was my task to show this objectively, to show how it functioned objectively. Now, the documents that I selected, which did not throw light on this question, were not utilised for any conclusions I made or, indeed, for my analysis. They do not deny the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and what happened in that war, but from it this has been separated. So that's what I dealt with, and that is why it is objective in that portion. Now, the fact that it was not considered cannot be a part of the report. So that is my position, which is now being altered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, don't worry about the part that you didn't see this. I hadn't seen this for -- until very recently myself. But could you help me out here and go over some of these VRS documents? It's --

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, as an expert, then, a security expert, I would need a comprehensive analysis, and I cannot make conclusions based on partial functions or how things were jeopardised because in the documents itself from the military aspect it is easily recognisable, and security has no better insight nor any better explanation than what command has. So nothing specific in security -- nothing more can be seen specifically within the realm of security than can be established through command and checked out through command. So my role is derived from the context of the material I dealt with, so I'm not concerned. I just don't have any qualified answers to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can't tell me why they blew up the -- or what security reasons there may have been for blowing up a water tank and blaming it on the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially not that. I can't say that. It is outside my knowledge and the possibilities that I have of clarifying the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this next document may bring the questions a little bit more into focus for you. Let's go to 65 ter 3500, and let me give you a good copy of that too. This is another document from the Drina Corps roughly three weeks later, June 21st, 1993. This one is actually from Milenko Zivanovic, the commander that gave the oral order to blow up the water tank and blame it on the Muslims. Now, having in mind that that particular order that General Zivanovic wanted this act to be blamed on the Muslims, let's take a look at what this says from Zivanovic to TG Pribicevac, to the command, attention Colonel Vukota Vukotic. Submit the data on the Muslim TGD that demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar. What's TDG mean? Or TDG? Those -- sorry, the initials.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand it that way. That's why I paused. Sabotage terrorist group. You quoted that correctly. Sabotage terrorist schools or diversionary terror -- tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we see this report and it starts, it says, Since we need to inform highest UNPROFOR bodies about the barbaric act of the Muslim DTG when they demolished the water supply system in Zeleni Jadar and on this occasion directly confronted our forces, inform me about the following. According to your estimate, how many terrorists took part in this demolition action; briefly describe the sequence of events, in the direct clash with our forces whether you killed, wounded heavily or lightly, or captured any terrorists. Submit identification data for these persons if you're in possession of any. Submit the data by June 21st, 1993, at the latest until 2 hours. Now, three weeks earlier Zivanovic tells Urosevic to demolish this thing, and it is to be presented to the public as if the Muslim forces did it. Now he's asking for documents suggesting -- or asking for how the Muslim forces did it. What's all this about in your view? Think the Muslim forces got in there and blew it up before the Serbs had a chance to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has already answered that when discussing the first document, and now after everything that has gone before, my colleague puts hypotheticals to the witness and documents and material that Mr. Vuga didn't deal with at all, so we are in a situation where we are dealing with hypothetical things and speculation and guess work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Assuming that these two documents are authentic, and I hear nothing challenging that so far, what Mr. McCloskey is doing is putting two apparently contradictory documents, and he's trying to solicit from the expert an explanation. So, Colonel, have you understood Mr. McCloskey's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood the question, but the whole idea of Colonel Milenko Zivanovic, I cannot find anything that would provide an answer to the question I'm being asked. Colonel Zivanovic knows about this, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I can tell you that has been established that the water system got blown up in this case, so I think a lot more people than Colonel Zivanovic know about it, but let me ask you a question. You have relied on many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment -- yes, okay. Go ahead, go ahead. One moment because we have got --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll hear the question out, Your Honour, and then afterwards I'll get on my feet if I need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have relied in your report and in your testimony on many VRS reports of Muslim terrorist actions. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, had you seen this particular report, 65 ter 3500, by itself, you would have assumed that -- as we would have all that read that, that this water tank was blown up by the Muslim forces and that this document was correct and genuine, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the document is correct and truthful, I cannot verify that, but I'm relying on what is written down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. My point is, if this is a completely fabricated document based on the orders of General Zivanovic to fabricate who actually blew up the water tank, doesn't that cause you a little concern about the rest of the documents you saw about blaming things on Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic? I suggest, anticipating what Ms. Nikolic probably would be saying, that, Colonel, you take off your headphones again, please. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't know whether this document has been fabricated or not by General Zivanovic, nor do we know what actually happened for the witness to be able to evaluate the document in the way in which my colleague put his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is very simple. I'm just putting an inference together from the previous document, nothing complicated nor unfair about it. Armies do this to each other all the time. That's my point. I'm just -- you know, and this has to do with security, counter-intelligence. It's right on point. Nothing mysterious about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have understood the question perfectly well, and on the basis of that, we believe that the witness can proceed to answer the question. That's unless he wants an explanation from Mr. McCloskey. So Mr. -- Colonel, have you understood the question that Mr. McCloskey put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood Mr. McCloskey's question. However, it would seem that what was not understood was what I dealt with, and I dealt with threats to the Army of Republika Srpska and the functions of the Army of Republika Srpska, any threat to that and jeopardy to that. So when my mission, my task, is placed in another context, in a different context, then it no longer has that same meaning. So that's the substance of the misunderstanding and the problem we are now facing. So, please, I would like to ask that my task and assignment, as I was given, should be assessed that way. As far as I'm concerned, this would be a completely new assignment as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have the authority to provide him a new assignment, but I will continue to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, part of testifying here is answering the questions. If the command in this courtroom allows the question to be asked, it's imperative for you to answer it whether it has to do with your report or not. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you rephrase the question the way you explained it when he had his headphones off, I think he will be able to answer it better, or he would choose to answer the question, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, the reason I'm asking you about this is because you have made reference to many VRS documents of this time period relating to what was going on in the woods around and in Srebrenica. Now, if we look at this document, it appears that this is a fake document designed to make the public and even the VRS believe that the Muslims blew up their own water tank, and so my concern is you've been reviewing a lot of documents. How do you know the difference between a faked document like this one, which as you can see created terrorists out of the blue sky, how do you know your -- the documents you looked at weren't fakes designed to mislead the public?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the word "fake" or "fabrication" is one that I did not utter. I did not say that the document was not in order, was not valid. All I said was that from the aspects of whether it was truthful or not I couldn't check that out, but I was looking at the contents of the document. So that was as far as the authenticity of the document is concerned, and I said that that is something General Zivanovic could know, but I am looking at the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more time, I'll try. What I'm fascinated with about this document is that it's sent to the command of Vukota Vukotic and it's talking about providing documents to your own army to provide support for what you know is a fantasy. Why would you want to fantasise with your own army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question goes quite beyond cross-examination and enters a different sphere altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't go beyond. I mean, the witness is being asked, from your experience as a military expert, would there be a reason or is there a reason why a Colonel like Milenko Zivanovic would draft such a document and have it addressed to and sent, communicated to colleague - I forgot his name now - Vukotic or Vukota Vukotic. That's -- and he can answer that. Yes, Colonel, if you could answer the question. Why would have Milenko Zivanovic drawn up and sent such a letter or communication to Vukota Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expert for security just like myself who deals in this area from this document cannot uncover the motives and reasons for which this, precisely at that time and in this way, was ordered by Zivanovic. Obviously, he wanted to achieve something through documents that were supposed to be given to him to his hand. Now, his intentions and the goal behind it, that stands behind that, is something I cannot uncover from this document, but the entire procedure as it stands in itself speaks of the fact that this is linked up. There was linkage between the document, the first document, and this second document. Now, the security organ cannot uncover the real reasons and go into what Milenko Zivanovic thought in doing so. So as far as I'm concerned, this procedure is not customary. It's unusual with respect to the way it was conducted, carried out, and I'm saying this because I can't say what Milenko Zivanovic's motives were in proceeding along these lines. I would have to have far greater insight into everything surrounding this particular act because this is insufficient for a conclusion to be made, but the procedure itself is unusual. I did not come across acts of this kind frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let's go to another document. It's one that you've seen briefly by the Defence, 65 ter number 1D1076. I'm sorry. My printing on this copy is really small, so maybe we can get a -- the one blown up on the screen to be a bit better. This is a document from February 11th, 1995, from the Drina Corps command, department of security and intelligence, from Vujadin Popovic. And I'm not so much interested in the information that was in it, and I think you've talked about that a -- but I see twice that Vujadin Popovic has made reference to the term "balija." It says, we have information that a man called Milorad Radocic [phoen] from Belgrade is in contact with the balija army." Then it goes on to say the balijas are trying to establish the whereabouts of prisoners. Now, this isn't a bar or the trenches or the back rooms or in some jeep. This is a document that goes out to all the security units, what looks like all the brigades of the Drina Corps. First of all, what is this term "balija," in your view?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the term "balija" represents a word in the vernacular that has a certain dose of -- it has a certain derogatory aspect or making fun of, just as the other side used the term "Chetniks," and you'll find similar terminology that was used when the parties were confronted, but it refers -- it's not too derogatory. It's mildly derogatory and appears in the vernacular. It has derogatory elements for referring to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of a worse word to Muslims than "balija"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a lot of terms, generally speaking. I nor my family were ever in areas where these mocking terms or derogatory terms were used throughout my upbringing and so on. So I'm not well-versed in the subject, and I was born in Croatia, as I said, and I never heard that used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You must have grown up in a different world than I did. What's worse, poturice or balija in your experience?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to context -- the context of these words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my learned friend to tell us what the object of that question is and what the grounds for asking it are and where he's heading. What parts of the examination-in-chief give rise to this type of question in the cross-examination, whether we are dealing with credibility or what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to answer that, Mr. McCloskey, in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He should probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you mind removing your headphones again, please? And be patient with us. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was a document that was brought up in direct examination. It was portrayed as a reasonable document involving counter-intelligence, is my recollection. There is -- we are in a case of genocide and persecutions where an ethnic element is part of it. As you have seen, these documents are laced with these terms, official VRS documents, and it's the position of the Prosecution that when you see documents -- when you see terms like this outside of the bar, outside of the trenches, when you see them in official documents, this has an effect on the troops and the morale of people that hear them. And it gives an indication of the professionalism and the quality and character of the people that write them. We are not prosecuting anyone for using rotten language, but I think the language gives us an insight into the ethnic feelings of those that write them and help us understand this case better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me consult with my colleagues and we'll -- yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to speak in my own language and answer the question. The witness has his headsets off, but [In English] I'll try English, but it's not good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the last thing we would do to you, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to express myself in the best way. I really don't think, Your Honour, that this witness is a real expert witness for the question like my colleague indeed asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, let me consult with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Simple solution to the problem, if it's a problem. This document was in the first place used by Mr. Zivanovic during his direct, to start with. Secondly, we find absolutely nothing extraordinary or out of the ordinary given the parameters of the expertise of this witness for this question to be put and answered. So I'm asking, Colonel -- page 55, line 4. One moment. Especially since the witness himself said that it is mildly derogatory and appears in the vernacular. So I'm going to ask the Colonel to put on his headphones. And yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm not quite sure where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither am I but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can get to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He had answered it from lines 8 to 12 -- to 11 of that page, page 55. And then you commented, actually. Your next question was, You must have grown up in a different world than I did. What's worse, then ... or balija in your experience, but you were stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I asked you, Colonel, what was worse, poturice or balija, in terms of a Muslim? How would -- what would be worse from a Muslim perspective? You grew up in Yugoslavia. You've got to know the answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To grow up in Yugoslavia in a microenvironment such as Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, these are two different matters, two different things. To answer your question precisely, I would have to have communications experience and experience in living in the environments where these terms are used, were these used in their original sense as slang and to know what the emotional connotations are, to know how people reacts to these terms. I didn't have such experience, so you can't put such a question to me as a Yugoslav. So this is why there is such a gap here. From books and other sources, there is much that I have learnt, but this is something that has to do with one's life experience, and I don't have that experience that relates to terms such as Chetniks and balijas and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to one more document, 65 ter 3497, and let me show you a copy of that. I won't spend much time with this one, Colonel. It's much like the last one. This is 29 April 1995 document to the chiefs of the organs for intelligence and security of -- looks like all the brigades, including the mixed artillery regiment and the Engineering Battalion, from Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. And just in looking at this, I count his use of the term balijas, it's actually in reference to a human being named Saban Omerovic [phoen], four times. Is it appropriate for a JNA-trained professional security officer to use these sorts of terms in their official correspondence with junior security officers who are looking to him as an example?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for how appropriate it is, if you're asking me this question, if you're putting this question to me as a professional, well, I can say that it's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I'm a security officer -- well, as I have already told you what my experience is, I won't go into these offices, but if I were such an officer I wouldn't understand all the dimensions and all the meanings or the various meanings of this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document, 65 ter 2517. This is really the last one of this group of documents. And I'll give you a -- so you can look at it. This is a document from 21 July 1995, personally to General Miletic from assistant commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir. It's entitled, "The Situation In Zepa." And what I'm mostly concerned about is paragraph 5. You've already told us who Tolimir is, and I want to get an idea from you why the -- what is it, if anything, about his position as chief of intel and security that would involve him in the activities we see suggested in paragraph 5. He's talking about the Muslim army here, in the beginning, crashing the enemy's defence as we see from paragraph 4, and he says, "The most convenient means for their destruction would be the uses of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs. Using these means would accelerate the surrender of Muslims and the fall of Zepa." Now, he's making this proposal to General Miletic. Is this the kind of getting around the -- how he's suggesting the destruction of the forces, is -- where in the security branch do we find rules supporting a -- you know, how to destroy the opposing forces? Is that something that fits into the definitions you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the definitions of special enemy groups and infiltrated groups. These forces don't have such a character. As to the means that were to be used, well, from the point of view of security, it wasn't something that was examined. It didn't fall within the scope of my work, and in itself this is not the task that falls within the field of that profession. This is a military task. I can't imagine what sort of chemical means are in question, but aerosol grenades and bombs, well, these means have not been banned. So the answer to the question is that I'm not familiar with the security aspect of this question. This is a military question, destroying enemy forces, special enemy forces that haven't been infiltrated. They are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what aerosol grenades and bombs are, the ones that have not been banned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I can't provide you with a classification of all the means, but on the basis of the literature I've consulted, I came across explanations according to which some of these means can be used, are not banned. So I can't provide you with a precise answer right now. I would have to prepare myself somewhat for such an answer, but I'm answering your question on the basis of what I have read so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you read or hear about what Mr. Butler said about what these things were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember what Mr. Butler said, but I'm not sure that I have linked up the answer with the question and answer, but I can't be very precise here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was I think on the witness stand even longer than you were, so don't worry about that. What kind of chemical weapons were in the arsenal of the JNA or VJ when you were chief assistant or you were the assistant chief of security?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got any experience or knowledge about chemical weapons. I'd been educated for PNKPO, anti-nuclear chemical protection -- defence, so from the point of view of defence. Not from the point of view of possessing means, but from that point of view we had enough information on protection on the way in which these means could be used to attack. I never had the occasion of seeing chemical or biological weapons nor did I study about how these weapons were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the last part of paragraph 5, we believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups of Muslim refugees fleeing from the direction of Stublic, Radava, and Brloska Planina: To your knowledge as a professional that's talked about the laws of war, is this legitimate, to try to destroy fleeing groups of refugees in order to get the army to surrender sooner?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order Stupcanica 95, it says that the Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not the target, and this isn't in accordance with that order or with any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is a very illegal order, isn't it? But it's not an order. Let's get that straight. This is a very illegal proposal.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposal, such as it is -- well, naturally it's not an order because General Tolimir did not have the authority to exercise command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it's very illegal, isn't it, this proposal, what he's asking for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that that was the case from the point of view of the order and from the point of view of the proposal itself, from the point of view of the order Stupcanica 95. That's what I had in mind when I referred to an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll have the break now. How much longer do you have, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's taken quite a bit longer than I thought it was going to, but I hope -- I'm still hoping I can finish today, but it's going to be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So 25 minutes -- do you want to reduce it to 20 minutes? Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could have waited to the end of the cross-examination of the Prosecutor, but I thought that it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the witness in the courtroom or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, pas du tout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Colonel, you can withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would require 25 minutes if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will give you 25 minutes. Yes, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it would be better to inform the parties and to ask your leave for this. Following some of the questions put by the Prosecutor, I would seek for your leave to allow me a very short cross-examination, which stems from the document that we've just seen a few moments ago, and also I have some questions with regarding Srebrenica. If you give me that permission, I will not go over -- I would need 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will communicate our decision on that later when we resume, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you had -- I think you were shown some documents and you talked a bit about the security officer's review of recruits or volunteers, I guess, from places outside the former Yugoslavia, in particular, Poland in this particular case. Remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we all understood that vetting foreign volunteers is a good idea for -- to make sure you're not -- try to make sure you're not getting some kind of a spy or problematic person. At that time, should or did -- well, let me put it this way: Would it have been a good idea for a VRS security officer in looking at a Polish volunteer to identify what religion he was from? Would religion be a significant issue in looking at his security -- potential security threat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This problem could be viewed from the aspects of the comprehensive conditions, not isolated, not religion and faith per se because that in itself, unless there are any other factors and influences, would not be an essential reason or vital reason from the security aspect. I don't know if I've been clear enough. From the security aspect, I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shouldn't a -- well, would a VRS security officer be worried about bringing on Polish Catholics?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A security officer would be worried, first and foremost, for the fact that there is no answer to the question as to what the real motives were of the arrival of volunteers because wars kill people; people are killed in wars, and so if somebody comes who is from -- comes in who is otherwise a very long way away from the war to take part in that war, then one must find the answer to what the real reason for that person doing that is. Now, if, along with that, there are some other factors, some other indexes which do not -- which cannot be incorporated into the entire context and character of the war, then this would require a comprehensive overview of the situation. So that would be an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. [Microphone not activated] ... documents now, and I want to go to a document that you talked a bit about, and I want to give you a -- another chance to answer a question on it. It's 65 ter 131, and for your benefit, let me give you a typed version of it. I'm sure you'll recognise it. It's that document that General Tolimir sent to General Gvero on the 13th of July, and we see it's handwritten, that it was submitted at 2230 hours on the 13th, so pretty late. You have given us your analysis of this, and I'm not going to ask you why Tolimir would suggest sending Muslims to take care of a pig farm, but I want you to look at that last line especially. "It would be best if this is a new group which has not been in contact with the other prisoners of war." Now, I'm going to ask you this question in the context of a hypothetical, which, as I mentioned, is -- should be fair game and part of your job here, and the hypothetical reflects the facts as the Prosecution sees them, and they are this: The late evening hours of 13 July, in the areas around Srebrenica and Bratunac, the morning of 13 July, about 16 people were taken by an execution squad in a bus when, buses were in great need, and executed. At about 1.00 p.m. the same day, on the 13 July, in the area near Konjevic Polje, three buses were taken from this massive transport of civilians and filled with Muslim men of military age and were joined by an APC and an excavator, and these three buses, the APC, and the excavator trundled off down the road to the Cerska Valley where the men in those buses were tied up, were summarily executed in the afternoon hours of 13 July, and later on a little bit later, roughly a thousand men in the warehouse at Kravica were mowed down by automatic weapon fire as they were huddled inside the warehouse. So that's what's happened on the 13 July, and at 2230 hours there is roughly somewhere in the amount of 5.000 to 6.000 Muslims all detained in schools and vehicles around Bratunac, some are actually in Zvornik, in the Orahovac school, that night. They are being beaten, they are being killed individually at times. So take that into account, that background. When you look at this document, and you've told us about Tolimir, that he's the man that should be in the know. And if Tolimir knows that there are hundreds and hundreds of prisoners being detained in separate areas, and he's talking about bringing 800 prisoners of war to this area at the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, "It would be best if this new group, which has not been in contact with the other prisoners of war." Now, given this factual scenario I've given you, what is the most reasonable interpretation of what that line means? Why would Tolimir want his group of 800 separate and apart from the other group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there are several things here. The description lasted a long time, so we must clarify them very well, properly. First of all, where was General Tolimir with respect to the events that we are discussing? That's the first serious question, for us to be able to see how far he actually was aware and informed of the events which were described or whether anything at all about those events reached General Tolimir at the place where he was located at the time. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me add something to make this clear, sorry. Let's say General Tolimir knew that those 6.000 men that were being held that were still alive were marked for death, were going to be summarily executed. If you throw that into the equation, let's say he knows, doesn't that give meaning to this last statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, and let us draw the conclusion if there is evidence to what you're saying, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to an easier area, Colonel, something I want to try to clear up. 65 ter number 107, and this is the Krivaja 95 attack plan that you saw. I think you said that you were nonplussed with a section in it that made reference to the security branch and the MPs finding locations for prisoners of war, and you talked at length about security branch and prisoners of war and MPs, and I don't want to go through that with you again, but I do want to give you a chance to see the original documents because I think that may help in your evaluation. Okay. The first one I want to give to you is -- just so it's clear it's ERN 04303386. It's got an original inked signature from General Zivanovic, and it was found in a -- what we call the Drina Corps archives. And in it at page 7 is that section that you talked about: "Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty." Now, to try to save some time, that one doesn't have any markings on it. It's got an original signature. I believe there was a suggestion that perhaps someone had corrected that mistaken view of the security branch's responsibilities in a later document. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If this is about P107, the ERN number that we have in e-court does not coincide with the ERN that Mr. McCloskey quoted on page 67, line 5. So could he please identify the document for us to be able to follow what it's about, if it's 507?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I've got it right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just the original inked copy of the Krivaja 95 plan. There are several of them. This is just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we know how many such documents the Prosecution has at its disposal. What does it mean, several of them? May we see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have the same number that you have. This is no big mystery. I can clear this up with you later, but it's -- this is all been disclosed. There is a Drina Corps version, and that's what we'll get into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to the list that I have, which the Prosecution provided for the cross-examination, P107 has a different ERN number from the one mentioned by Mr. McCloskey. So could we see it -- see whether it's the same document and then move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The one in e-court is -- was picked up at the Zvornik Brigade. The one the Colonel has came from the Drina Corps collection. Somebody want to see it? They're welcome to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed? I don't understand why we should have this problem, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is really nothing very mysterious about this, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you will show the document or you give the information later to the parties. In the meantime, please, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. So that's the one that's got that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of two versions of these documents. One of them was corrected, and it was subject of my examination of the witness and the cross-examination of many other witnesses. And I'd like to know if the Prosecution has the third or fourth or any other version of these documents as well. I'd like to see that. And this ERN number is not the same as the ERN number indicated to us through document 107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm into ERN knots all day long, but it's -- I'm going to get to the document that he's concerned about, and these documents have all been provided for -- to the Defence in various ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed and then you clarify this later with the parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, we have got that original, inked version now, and that should have gone out via teletype or in some other way to various -- the various brigade units, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something that doesn't quite tally. You said it was page 7. I have page 4 here. It refers to security. So we are talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's that section you testified about. Thanks for the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness has this document shown to him in a binder, our binder, and it is not necessary to look at this document given right now by the Prosecution. It is P107, and I do not see any -- any problem to see that in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to see the document that he has been given, of course you have every right to have a look at it and confront it with what you may have given him, but please, let's proceed. Do you wish to see the document that he's just been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please show the document to Mr. Zivanovic? And in the meantime, you can proceed on the basis of what you have on the screen in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right, Colonel. So let's say we see this original, inked signature of that document. That should be valid, though you've pointed out to a document that Mr. Zivanovic went over with you that had what you said I think dark line-outs. So let me show you the original of that document, and that was 65 ter 1D382. And here is the original, and Mr. Zivanovic, if you'd like to see it, you can see the pencil marks on it. It's just the original of the photocopy that everybody's had. Let me give that to you so you can see it. It's -- as an expert, as you probably agree, it's always good to be able to have original documents when making some kind of analysis. Just take a look at that, and you'll see those pencil marks that you've seen -- oh, sorry, that's not the pencil-marked one. It's getting late. We are -- that's -- sorry, that's the original that you were looking at or that's the inked copy. This one that has the pencil marks, I'm sure you'll recognise it as the -- an original version of the copy that you were talking about, but there is no inked signature at the bottom. And the important part of all this time is, I want you to be able to look at, which may not have been clear in the copied version, the last page of the marked-up version that says -- stamped, it was a command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Isn't that a receipt stamp, showing that that was received by the Bratunac Brigade on 5 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question? I was reading the document, so I wasn't quite following. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you see that receipt stamp at the bottom that shows that this document came it to the Bratunac Brigade on 5 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I can see the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now, if we take into account that this document was received by the Bratunac Brigade on the 5th of July, and now we look at these pencil marks on it, isn't it a fair conclusion that somebody at the Bratunac Brigade went through the security section and added a few things and crossed out a few things?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the designation of the document, one could come to the conclusion that this was done in the Bratunac Brigade, given the marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see, as you've testified to, I think, that in the marked-up version of that document somebody wrote in that Pribicevac as the location where POWs would go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is obvious in the document. You can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we go to P3025, we may not need to get it all up on the board, but if it comes up, fine. This is what you were shown earlier, and it's the Bratunac Brigade's version of the Krivaja attack plan dated 5 July where they adopted much of the information in the corps plan and made it applicable to their specific needs as a brigade, which I think you've testified about. And we should see on that that they've actually put in prisoners of war and war booty to be collected in Pribicevac. So the point of that would be that if we see the original inked signature of Milenko Zivanovic, would that reflect the final work product of the Drina Corps as it went out to the brigades?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question mentions a request for fighting. It's from -- it's forwarded to the subordinate units, and that includes the Bratunac Brigade. So it's a basis for the commander. The commander will take a decision on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right. And the part that you were nonplussed with or you thought was inappropriate in terms of the use of security was that portion that said "security organs and the military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty". So my question is now that you understand how that carved-up document came into existence and that you can see that the original words of General Zivanovic or the people that drafted it for him are not changed, do you still disagree or are you still nonplussed by this comment, "Security organs and military police will indicate the areas for gathering and securing prisoners of war"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two documents. Which one are you referring to right now? I have the original document from General Zivanovic, and I have a document that has been amended, so could you be precise, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The original document from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. The original document, which was drafted and signed by General Zivanovic, well, I examined it in the light of the norms in force at the time, and this has to do with engaging security organs, and in the light of those norms and regulations, well, I'll tell you what it involves if you like, but in the light of those norms and regulations, this document or this part of the document wasn't in accordance with the regulations in force at the time in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we adjourn early now? I need to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. By all means. Colonel, we haven't finished today contrary to our expectations. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. You can withdraw now with the assistance of our usher. In the meantime, before we adjourn, Mr. McCloskey, on something completely different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thanks. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.
